lede: Human insulin can be made by bacteria that carry a human gene. It takes an enzyme that cuts DNA at one sequence, a small ring of bacterial DNA to carry the gene, and a tank of multiplying bacteria. Every stage has one name the exam asks for, and one stage asks you to count.
can: Describe the stages of making human insulin in order, with the name for each one.
Find where a restriction enzyme cuts a base sequence, and count the sections it leaves.
Explain why one enzyme cuts both the gene and the plasmid, and what downstreaming is for.

md: Your pancreas makes insulin every time your blood glucose rises. Someone with type 1 diabetes cannot, so they inject it, and what they inject can be human insulin made by bacteria. Getting a bacterium to make a human protein takes one gene, two cuts, one join and a very large tank.

alt: Six stages: a restriction enzyme cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA; the same enzyme opens a plasmid; the gene is joined into it; the plasmid goes into a bacterium; the bacteria multiply in a fermenter; the insulin is extracted, purified and packaged.

md:
An organism's **genome** is all of its genetic material. **Genetic engineering** changes the genome to give the organism a **desirable characteristic** it did not have.

A **gene** is a section of DNA that codes for one protein, and insulin is a protein. Move the human insulin gene into a bacterium, and the bacterium makes human insulin.

prompt: What is the genome of an organism?
options: the protein one gene codes for
explain: All of its genetic material. A gene is one section of it, and the protein is what a gene codes for.

md:
A **restriction enzyme** cuts DNA only where it finds one particular **base sequence**. Each enzyme has its own sequence, and a question always tells you which. The enzyme in this lesson looks for TCGA.

It cuts the top strand between T and C, and the bottom strand two bases further along. This **staggered cut** leaves a few unpaired bases hanging off each end: **sticky ends**.

title: Why the ends are sticky
md: The unpaired bases on one end are complementary to the unpaired bases on the other: C pairs with G and G with C. So any two ends this enzyme leaves can pair up again, like the two halves of a zip.

prompt: The short single-stranded ends left by a restriction enzyme's staggered cut are called ______ ends.
explain: Sticky ends. Describing them as loose or matching is true, but the mark is for the name.

md:
**Worked example.** Into how many sections is this length of DNA cut?
**Step 1: find every site.** Read the top strand from the left. TCGA appears at bases 3 to 6 and 11 to 14.
**Step 2: one site, one staggered cut.** The bottom strand under each site reads TCGA from right to left, so it is cut too, two bases along: 2 cuts.
**Step 3: count the sections.** A straight length already has two ends, so every cut adds a section: 2 + 1 = **3 sections**.

prompt: The same enzyme cuts between T and C wherever the top strand reads TCGA. This top strand reads ACTCGATTGTCGACTTCGAG. Into how many sections is this length of DNA cut?
explain: TCGA appears 3 times, at bases 3 to 6, 10 to 13 and 16 to 19, so there are 3 staggered cuts and 3 + 1 = 4 sections.

md: A **plasmid** is a small ring of DNA in a bacterium, separate from its chromosome. The **same restriction enzyme** cuts the plasmid open. It cuts at the same base sequence, so the plasmid's sticky ends are **complementary** to the gene's. The gene pairs into the gap and is joined in. The ring that results is a **recombinant plasmid**.

alt: A straight piece of DNA cut in 3 places falls into 4 numbered pieces; a circular plasmid cut in 3 places falls into 3.

md: That is why one cut is enough for the plasmid: it opens the ring without breaking it into pieces. On a ring, n cuts give n pieces; on a straight length, n cuts give n + 1.

prompt: Why is the plasmid cut with the same restriction enzyme that cut out the insulin gene?
options: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
so the enzyme is used up
so the plasmid falls into many pieces
answer: so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join
explain: Same enzyme, same base sequence, complementary sticky ends. A different enzyme would leave ends that do not pair.

text: 5. Into a bacterium, then a fermenter

md:
The recombinant plasmid is put into a bacterium, which is now **genetically modified**. The modified bacteria are grown in a **fermenter**. There the bacteria **multiply**, their plasmids are copied each time, and every bacterium uses the human gene to make **human insulin**.

Insulin is a **protein**, so the bacterium builds it from **amino acids**, in the order the gene codes for.

title: The gene, not the hormone
md: Summer 2024's report names this: answers saying the plasmid contained the hormone could not score. The plasmid carries the **insulin gene**. The insulin does not exist until the bacterium makes it.

prompt: In the fermenter, what happens to the genetically modified bacteria and their plasmids?
explain: They multiply, or reproduce. Purifying comes later, and the cutting was done before the plasmid went into the bacterium.

md: At the end the fermenter holds a broth of bacteria, leftover food, waste and insulin. **Downstreaming** turns it into a medicine in three stages: **extraction** (take the insulin out), **purification** (remove everything that is not insulin) and **packaging**. It is needed so that a **pure** form of insulin, safe to inject, reaches the patient.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Genetic Engineering"
why: A short lesson on genetic engineering, made for another exam board: read the note beside it before you watch.

title: What other boards add, and what they leave out
md: Clips made for the other boards usually spend time on **GM crops** and name **ligase**, an enzyme that joins the ends. CCEA asks for neither. They often stop before the **fermenter** and **downstreaming**, which CCEA does ask for, so learn those from this lesson.

prompt: The three stages of downstreaming, in order, are extraction, ______ and packaging.
explain: Purification: everything that is not insulin is removed, so the product is pure and safe to inject.

caption: Each advantage answers a problem with the old way.

md: Insulin used to be extracted from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Insulin from bacteria is **identical to human insulin**, it can be made in **large quantities**, it is **cheaper**, and **no animal is used**, so people with ethical or religious objections to animal products can use it.

prompt: Which of these is an advantage of making insulin with genetically modified bacteria?
options: it is identical to human insulin
it needs no genes at all
it is made without any protein
answer: it is identical to human insulin
explain: Identical to human insulin. The other advantages are large quantities, lower cost, and no animal being used.

md:
Say what the **genome** is and why genetic engineering changes it.
Give the stages of making human insulin in order: cut, join, insert, **fermenter**, **downstreaming**.
Find a restriction enzyme's sites in a base sequence, mark each **staggered cut**, and count the sections.
Explain why the **same enzyme** cuts the gene and the plasmid, and say the plasmid carries the **gene**, not the hormone.
Give the advantages of insulin made this way.

This is a Higher question near the end of B2, often seven to ten marks. It opens with one-mark names: genome, restriction enzyme, sticky ends, downstreaming. The later marks ask you to explain a stage or to work on a base sequence. Stuck on a describe question? Write the stages in order, one short sentence each, and name the tool at every stage.
